title: Three good things
hookLine: writing three good things each night was linked to more happiness in a 2005 study (Seligman et al.), with modest effects

cards: Here's something your brain does without asking. At the end of the day, it hands you a summary, and the summary is biased. The rude driver makes the highlights.
So does the late bus. The perfectly fine lunch, the stranger who held the door, the song you liked on the radio: cut for time.
Psychologists call this lean toward the bad the negativity bias, and it's probably kept our ancestors alive. But it doesn't make for a fair report.
A new week, on gratitude, starts with an exercise simple enough to seem silly.

teach.b: In 2005, the psychologist Martin Seligman and his colleagues at the University of Pennsylvania ran an online study of several simple exercises.
In one, every night for a week, you write down three things that went well today, and for each one, why it happened. No journal, no ritual. Three things and a reason.
Compared with a placebo exercise, writing about early memories, the three good things group reported being a bit happier and a bit less depressed.
Here's the surprise: the difference was still showing six months later, especially in people who kept doing it on their own. Now, the honest part.
The effects were modest. Later studies have found smaller, mixed results, and nobody should expect a nightly list to fix a hard life.
It isn't a cure, and gratitude forced on someone in pain can hurt; that comes back later this week. But the exercise does something clever. It works directly against the bias.
The brain's summary cuts the good bits; this puts them back in. And the second half, why did it happen, matters.
It makes you notice the causes: that you asked for help, that a friend thought of you, that you went outside.
Good luck becomes something you can see, and sometimes repeat. Many traditions teach gratitude as a duty or a prayer. This one is a small experiment anyone can run, on the back of a receipt.

how: The three good things exercise is widely used in positive psychology courses and therapy: each night for a week or longer, people write three things that went well that day and why each happened.

practice: Look back over the last day and find one thing that went well; small counts, a good coffee, a text, a moment of quiet. Ask why it happened, and stay with it a breath or two. Then find a second, and a third, each with its why.
